publication: MIT OpenCourseWare, MIT Sloan School of Management (graduate course materials)

verified.evidence: Course number, title, term (Spring 2001), instructor (Prof. Mary Rowe), graduate level and Sloan School affiliation matched on ocw.mit.edu (course home, lecture notes, readings and assignments pages). Sitewide CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license matched on ocw.mit.edu/pages/privacy-and-terms-of-use/.

summary: An archived MIT Sloan graduate course that teaches negotiation theory in employment settings, with eleven topic sessions built around role-play simulations. It treats conflict from both the first-party (negotiator) and third-party (mediator, arbitrator) perspectives and includes difficult workplace situations. The posted materials include lecture notes, simulations, self-assessments and assignment instructions.
arguments: Negotiation skill is built through repeated simulation, self-assessment and analysis of others’ negotiations, not through reading alone.
Conflict management in organizations includes third-party options such as mediation and arbitration, not only direct bargaining.
Workplace conflicts such as whistle-blowing and discrimination complaints require procedures and due process, not just bargaining tactics.
strengths: Real graduate course materials from a business school, openly licensed; emphasizes practice, self-assessment and workplace conflict systems, which most negotiation primers omit.
limitations: Materials date from 2001; several assigned books (for example Getting to Yes) and course-pack readings are copyrighted and not included on OCW. It is a course archive, not an evidence review.
generalizability: High for organizational settings: the employment-relations focus transfers directly to staff, vendor and internal resource negotiations, including in sports organizations.
relevance: The owner named this course as a starting example. It supplies open simulations and a conflict-systems view that complement Week 7 (negotiation) and the dispute-resolution material in Week 11.

title: Introduction to Psychology (PSYC 110, Spring 2007)
publication: Open Yale Courses, Yale University (recorded lecture course)
license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (Open Yale Courses terms of use); third-party content is excluded unless a lecture’s Credits section says otherwise. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Course number, title, instructor (Paul Bloom) and recording term (Spring 2007) matched on oyc.yale.edu course and lecture pages; license (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, third-party exclusion) matched on oyc.yale.edu/terms and the course page.

summary: A full recorded Yale undergraduate survey of psychology, with lectures on foundations (including Freud), cognition, development, emotion, social behavior and the psychology of the good life. It is a broad, accessible map of the discipline taught by a prominent researcher. Lecture videos and transcripts are openly available.
arguments: Human behavior is best understood by combining evolutionary, cognitive, developmental and social explanations rather than any single lens.
Emotion and reason are intertwined; emotions are not simply errors in an otherwise rational system.
Some historically influential theories (for example, Freud’s) are presented for their influence, not as current scientific consensus.
strengths: Complete, openly licensed lecture series with transcripts; strong on the conceptual map of the field.
limitations: Recorded in 2007, before the replication crisis reshaped parts of social psychology; some findings presented then (for example in priming research) need to be checked against later replications. Introductory level.
contested: Parts of the social-psychology canon covered in introductory courses of this period have since failed large replication attempts; APERTURE flags these in the relevant weeks.
generalizability: Moderate: it builds vocabulary and theory, but organizational transfer requires the applied and replication-aware material in Weeks 1–3.
relevance: The owner named this course as a starting example. It is the open foundation for the behavioral-science school (Weeks 1–3) for a learner without formal psychology training.

verified.evidence: Title, authors (David S. Bright, Anastasia H. Cortes), publisher (OpenStax) and publication date (March 20, 2019) matched on openstax.org details, preface and chapter pages; license wording (CC BY-NC-SA) matched on openstax.org chapter pages.

summary: An openly licensed introductory management textbook with chapters written by subject specialists. It covers the manager’s functions, organizational structure and change, strategy, decision-making, leadership, teams and the external environment. It is a survey text suited to building vocabulary before graduate readings.
arguments: Management can be organized around planning, organizing, leading and controlling, while recognizing that real managerial work is less tidy than that frame.
Structure, strategy and culture interact; changing one without the others tends to fail.
Decision-making in organizations is bounded by information, time and cognitive limits.
strengths: Free, complete, editable for noncommercial use; broad coverage with key-term lists for review.
limitations: Undergraduate survey level; evidence strength is not graded chapter by chapter, and some practitioner frameworks appear alongside research findings without distinction.
generalizability: Broad and general; useful as a reference across Weeks 5, 8, 9 and 12, with APERTURE adding evidence grading.
relevance: An open alternative to proprietary MBA-core management texts; it backs the foundation-mode prerequisites in the business school weeks.

summary: An openly licensed organizational behavior textbook covering individual differences, perception, motivation, groups and teams, communication, power and politics, leadership, organizational structure, culture and change. Each chapter includes key terms and critical-thinking cases.
arguments: Behavior in organizations is shaped by individual, group and organizational-level factors at once.
Motivation, power and culture are levers managers can study systematically rather than treat as intuition.
Organizational change requires attention to resistance and to the informal system, not only formal structure.
strengths: Free, complete OB survey from established authors; maps closely onto MBA leadership and organizational behavior cores.
limitations: Survey level; does not consistently report effect sizes or replication status, so popular ideas sit next to well-replicated findings.
generalizability: Broad; supports Weeks 2, 5, 6 and 8 as an open reference, with APERTURE adding evidence-strength labels.
relevance: An open counterpart to the organizational behavior and leadership core courses that every MBA reference program requires.

license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per the openstax.org preface and book pages (some chapter pages in search results showed a plain Creative Commons Attribution notice). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, senior contributing authors (Julie Dahlquist, Rainford Knight), publisher (OpenStax) and publish date (March 24, 2022) matched on openstax.org details, preface and index pages; license (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) matched on the preface, with conflicting notices on some chapter pages.

summary: An openly licensed introductory finance textbook covering financial statements, the time value of money, valuation, risk and return, capital budgeting, cost of capital and financial planning. It is written for readers without prior finance training.
arguments: Value depends on the timing and risk of cash flows, which is why discounting and net present value sit at the center of investment decisions.
Financial statements are tools for analysis, not just compliance documents.
Capital budgeting choices should be compared against the opportunity cost of capital.
strengths: Free, current (2022) and structured for self-study; covers the corporate-finance and accounting foundations found in every MBA reference core.
limitations: Introductory; less depth than an MBA corporate-finance course on capital structure and valuation under uncertainty.
generalizability: High: finance tools are domain-general and apply directly to budgeting and capital allocation in sports organizations.
relevance: The open backbone for Week 10 and for the budget model in the Week 14 capstone.

summary: An archived MIT Sloan graduate course on structured team projects, published on MIT OpenCourseWare with a page on its pedagogy. APERTURE lists it as an open example of how a business school structures team-based applied work; its specific contents were not confirmed in search results.
arguments: Business schools treat team project work as a designed learning experience with its own pedagogy, not an add-on.
Applied team projects are a common way to integrate core-course concepts.
strengths: Open, from an MBA program in the reference set; shows how project-based integration is organized.
limitations: Only title, number, term and level were confirmed; materials are from 2003 and their content and completeness were not verified.
